The ère actiaque, as Proudhon calls it—the Actian age, at the origin of our own age?
Every word of this chapter of Tacitus is completely contemporary:
Great minds fell silent. I begin a work rich in disasters, terrible in battles, torn by seditions, savage even in peace.
Civil and foreign wars were for the most part intertwined.
The combination of foreign war and civil war is not rhetoric. It is the terrible reality itself, recognized and spoken aloud: the inability to distinguish war from peace.
The inability to distinguish war from peace is at the same time fas nefasque mixtum: right and wrong mixed together.

Came across James Shotwell’s Berlin lecture of March 1927—which Ernst Jäckh calls the “formal introduction” to the new understanding of war, with its treatment of the aggressor as a criminal:
“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?”
From a repetitive understanding of the world toward science, democracy, and goals that were once achieved through war. We should add: now achieved in other ways.
The Industrial Revolution is very important here.
Change takes the place of repetition.
In the past, the world was “static” and there were wars. Now it is becoming dynamic, and supposedly there is to be peace.

Rage and a bad conscience go looking for someone to blame, for a scapegoat. And there will always be fools and idiots ready to walk straight into the knife and satisfy that need. That too belongs to the dynamism of the new world age.
War is no longer the ultima ratio—the final resort. It has lost its reason for existing.

“This new dynamic world, created by the human mind, has no other means of defending itself against this advance of destruction through war, and of saving its most precious inheritance”—what exactly is this most precious inheritance?—“than the very technology on which it both depends and through which it puts itself in danger, since every new discovery forces the enemy to produce something equal to it, or even more terrible.” That is what the war of 1914–18 revealed to us. It showed us clearly that this was not an accident but something typical, and that it would become more and more so as civilization continued to develop.
But what does that actually mean?
The more terrible the weapons become, the less respect they leave for the enemy. That is what is new: the enemy is disqualified more and more completely.
What follows from this? asks J. Shotwell.

His answer: because war has stopped being predictable—as it supposedly was in the static, repetitive age—it no longer belongs to Realpolitik. We must therefore develop a Realpolitik of peace: the League of Nations, international justice, Locarno.
My view is different. Because war has stopped being predictable, it does not therefore have to stop existing.
War was always a judgment of God and therefore always unpredictable.

The real question is whether enmity has disappeared. Unfortunately, it has not. And if war no longer belongs to the Realpolitik of the old kind, perhaps that simply means that, as the form and substance of war change, the meaning and substance of Realpolitik must change as well.
Perhaps politics can no longer be merely the nineteenth-century “art of what is possible and predictable.”

Perhaps precisely the desire to save our most precious inheritance, precisely the awareness that we are living through an enormous turning point, precisely the dynamic character of the present, precisely our awareness that war has become incalculable—perhaps all of this will produce a new kind of Realpolitik.

A Realpolitik that includes this awareness within itself, and that does not fear matching the other side’s willingness to face danger with an equal willingness of its own, provided it knows that it possesses the right weapons.

The spiritus malignus, the magnus deceptor—the evil spirit, the great deceiver—whom Descartes speaks of pursues me too.
His great trick is to awaken in us the fear that deception is unavoidable, that all human existence is ultimately exposed to fraud.
The thief who shouts “Stop, thief!” is a fairly harmless figure compared with the deceiver who whispers into our ear that we are so terribly easy to deceive.
Descartes knew this most sinister of all deceivers.
Ah yes: sum, sum, sum—little bee, buzz around.
Descartes still tried to deal with this woodworm by means of an ergo.
We can no longer argue our way out of it with an ergo. We cannot even escape it by praying as our parents taught us to pray. There is nothing left but the sign of the Cross.
